entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5246"/><div sID="gen7825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5246"/>3. Rather, explanatory of "this" in <reference osisRef="Job.35.2">Job 35:2</reference>, "That thou sayest (to thyself, as if a distinct person) What advantage is it (thy integrity) to thee? What profit have I (by integrity) more than (I should have) by my sin?" that is, more than if I had sinned (<reference osisRef="Job.34.9">Job 34:9</reference>). Job had said that the wicked, who use these very words, do not suffer for it (<reference osisRef="Job.21.13-Job.21.15">Job 21:13-15</reference>); whereby he virtually sanctioned their sentiments. The same change of persons from oblique to direct address occurs (<reference osisRef="Job.19.28">Job 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.17">22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7825" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 3. Rather, explanatory of "this" in Job 35:2 , "That thou sayest (to thyself, as if a distinct person) What advantage is it (thy integrity) to thee? What profit have I (by integrity) more than (I should have) by my sin?" that is, more than if I had sinned ( Job 34:9 ). Job had said that the wicked, who use these very words, do not suffer for it ( Job 21:13-15 ); whereby he virtually sanctioned their sentiments. The same change of persons from oblique to direct address occurs ( Job 19:28 ; 22:17 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5248"/><div sID="gen7827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5248"/>5-8. Elihu like Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.3.12">3, 12</reference>) shows that God is too exalted in nature to be susceptible of benefit or hurt from the righteousness or sin of men respectively; it is themselves that they benefit by righteousness, or hurt by sin.<div eID="gen7827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold the clouds, which are higher than thou--</hi>spoken with irony. Not only are they higher than thou, but thou canst not even reach them clearly with the eye. Yet these are not as high as God's seat. God is therefore too exalted to be dependent on man. Therefore He has no inducement to injustice in His dealings with man. When He afflicts, it must be from a different motive; namely, the good of the sufferer. <div eID="gen7828" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5252"/><div sID="gen7833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5252"/>10-13. But the reason is that the innocent sufferers often do not humbly seek God for succor; so to their "pride" is to be laid the blame of their ruin; also because (<reference osisRef="Job.35.13-Job.35.16">Job 35:13-16</reference>) they, as Job, instead of waiting God's time in pious trust, are prone to despair of His justice, when it is not immediately visible (<reference osisRef="Job.33.19-Job.33.26">Job 33:19-26</reference>). If the sufferer would apply to God with a humbled, penitent spirit, He would hear.<div eID="gen7833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Where, &c.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jr 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.13">Is 51:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">songs--</hi>of joy at deliverance (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.8">Psa 42:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.149.5">149:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.25">Ac 16:25</reference>).<div eID="gen7835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the night--</hi>unexpectedly (<reference osisRef="Job.34.20">Job 34:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.25">25</reference>). Rather, "in calamity." <div eID="gen7836" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5256"/><div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5256"/><hi type="bold">14. Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him--</hi>(as a temporal deliverer; for he did look for a Redeemer after death, <reference osisRef="Job.19.25-Job.19.27">Job 19:25-27</reference>; which passage cannot consistently with Elihu's assertion here be interpreted of "seeing" a temporal "redeemer"), <reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.11">9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.3">23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">8, 9</reference>; yet, judgment ... ; therefore trust ... But the Hebrew favors Maurer, "How much less (will God ... regard, <reference osisRef="Job.35.13">Job 35:13</reference>), since thou sayest, that He does not regard thee." So in <reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>. Thus Elihu alludes to Job's words (<reference osisRef="Job.19.7">Job 19:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.20">30:20</reference>).<div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>that is, thy cause, thy right; as in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Pr 31:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">8</reference>.<div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trust--</hi>rather, "wait thou" on Him, patiently, until He take up thy cause (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.7">Psa 37:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 14. Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him-- (as a temporal deliverer; for he did look for a Redeemer after death, Job 19:25-27 ; which passage cannot consistently with Elihu's assertion here be interpreted of "seeing" a temporal "redeemer"), Job 7:7 ; 9:11 ; 23:3 , 8, 9 ; yet, judgment ... ; therefore trust ... But the Hebrew favors Maurer, "How much less (will God ... regard, Job 35:13 ), since thou sayest, that He does not regard thee." So in Job 4:19 . Thus Elihu alludes to Job's words ( Job 19:7 ; 30:20 ). judgment-- that is, thy cause, thy right; as in Psa 9:16 ; Pr 31:5 , 8 . trust-- rather, "wait thou" on Him, patiently, until He take up thy cause ( Psa 37:7 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5257"/><div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5257"/>15. As it is, because Job waited not trustingly and patiently (<reference osisRef="Job.35.14">Job 35:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.20.12">Nu 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.2">Zep 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>), God hath visited ... ; yet still he has not taken (severe) cognizance of the great multitude (English Version wrongly, "extremity") of sins; therefore Job should not complain of being punished with undue severity (<reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">11:6</reference>). Maurer translates: "Because His anger hath not visited (hath not immediately punished Job for his impious complaints), nor has He taken strict (great) cognizance of his folly (sinful speeches); therefore," &c. For "folly," Umbreit translates with the Rabbins, "multitude." Gesenius reads with the Septuagint and Vulgate needlessly, "transgression." <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/>
